title: India Conquered Cannes 2026 — But Anurag Kashyap Wants You to Ask Why Nobody Watched the Films
excerpt: From Alia Bhatt million-like looks to Diana Penty golden saree tribute, Indian stars lit up the French Riviera. Then Anurag Kashyap asked the question nobody wanted to hear.
body:
The 2026 Cannes Film Festival wrapped its first week with India occupying more visual real estate on the Croisette than perhaps any year before. But behind the couture gowns and diamond-studded red carpet walks, a familiar tension played out — one that cuts to the heart of how India engages with the world's most prestigious cinema gathering.

## The Fashion Blitz

**Alia Bhatt** kicked things off with two back-to-back looks that collectively pulled over 1.9 million Instagram likes within hours. Her appearances — one a sculptural, architectural piece, the other softer and more romantic — became the most-discussed Indian moments of the festival's opening days. For NRIs scrolling through their feeds from New York to London to Toronto, it was a reminder of just how thoroughly Bollywood's biggest names have cracked the global red carpet code.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DYTv7YcjDiI/

**Aditi Rao Hydari**, fresh off her breakout year in Indian cinema, brought something different entirely. Her Cannes wardrobe was a masterclass in range — a breezy black-and-white Riviera maxi dress one moment, a custom champagne silk Chaarbagh saree by JADE by MK the next. The saree, inspired by Mughal gardens and archival block prints, drew widespread praise for blending Indian heritage with red carpet sophistication. She capped it with a neon metallic green Tony Ward Couture gown that was pure fashion risk — and it paid off.

**Diana Penty** made her third consecutive Cannes appearance, this time with a double act that might have been the week's most pointed cultural statement. At the Bharat Pavilion, she appeared in a custom golden knit saree by Manish Malhotra — shimmering metallic textures, sculpted puff sleeves, and a plunging neckline that updated the six-yard drape for global fashion audiences. "Cannes dipped in a little Indian gold," she captioned her post, adding that gold symbolises far more than colour in India. Later that evening, she pivoted to an avant-garde crimson gown by Amit Aggarwal, featuring engineered Ikat textures and a futuristic metallic sheen — Indian textile heritage reimagined as wearable art.

## Anurag Kashyap's Reality Check

Then came the cold water.

Filmmaker **Anurag Kashyap**, speaking to critic Sucharita Tyagi at the festival, delivered a blunt assessment of what India's Cannes obsession actually looks like from inside the tent.

"In India, the problem and obsession with Cannes is only to walk the red carpet," Kashyap said. "They don't understand there's a festival and the purpose of it is beyond the red carpet."

He went further: "What is more important is the cinema, and I don't think people even come here for cinema. Even all the Indian people who are coming to the market are not watching films. Very rarely I see someone."

The comments cut to a real structural gap. According to Kashyap, Indian producers often fear festival circuits, struggle with submission timelines, and lose opportunities because they're "never in time." Only a handful of Indian films made official selections this year — a fraction of what the country's output could represent on the global stage.

## The Numbers Game NRIs Should Care About

For the diaspora, Cannes has long been a source of pride — Indian names on global stages, Indian designers dressing the Croisette, Indian faces in international media cycles. But Kashyap's critique lands differently when you consider the economics. India produces over 1,500 films annually across languages. France produces roughly 300. Yet France's festival presence dwarfs India's.

The co-production angle is evolving, though. Producer Eram Faridi of Erams Entertainment used this year's festival to push international collaborations, emphasising storytelling partnerships across more than 140 countries. It's a model the Indian film industry has been slow to adopt but one that could finally position Indian cinema as a global production partner, not just a red carpet presence.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

If you're an NRI who cheered Alia Bhatt's Cannes looks on Instagram, you're not wrong to celebrate — Indian representation on the world's most photographed staircase matters. But if you also want Indian cinema to be *seen* at Cannes, not just *worn* there, Kashyap's words are worth sitting with.

The good news: Indian designers like Manish Malhotra, Amit Aggarwal, and JADE by MK are building genuine global credibility through these appearances. The fashion pipeline is working. The cinema pipeline has catching up to do.

Cannes 2026 proved India can dominate the spectacle. The question is whether it's ready to dominate the programme.
